title: Trump Promise Dashboard Showed Only About 19% Marked as Kept
description_short: Trump Promise Dashboard Showed Only About 19% Marked as Kept
description_medium: PBS reported that roughly 19% of tracked promises were rated as kept, a figure far below Trump's broad claim of near-total completion. Percentage framing matters because it strips away anecdotal victories and shows aggregate delivery performance. The number became a measurable counterweight to speech-driven success narratives.
description_long: On February 27, 2026, PBS compared Donald Trump’s claim that he had kept all of his campaign promises with PolitiFact’s MAGA-Meter, which tracks individual pledges against measurable outcomes. At that point, about 19% of the promises were marked kept, roughly 45% were in progress, and three were classified as compromises. The categories matter: a pledge still underway was not counted as either complete or abandoned, while a compromise represented partial fulfillment. The tracker counted Trump’s January 6 pardons and the 2025 extension of earlier tax cuts as kept promises. It rated his pledge to eliminate taxes on Social Security benefits as a compromise because the 2025 tax law created a limited break for people over 65 through 2028 rather than ending taxes for all Social Security recipients. The 19% figure is a dated snapshot of the promises PolitiFact was tracking before the State of the Union. It does not mean that the other promises had all failed, and it is not an independent audit of every claim Trump made about his record.

title: Trump: Middle East attacks intensify as Trump says he rejects Iran’s attempt to talk
description_short: Trump: Middle East attacks intensify as Trump says he rejects Iran’s attempt to talk
description_medium: Middle East attacks intensify as Trump says he rejects Iran’s attempt to talk. US president claims ‘they want to talk. I said: Too Late!’, while Rubio threatens the ‘hardest hits are yet to come’ This entry is cataloged as a standalone event because it captures a concrete action, public statement, or policy consequence linked directly to Trump. The downstream effects include elevated institutional stress, public-trust erosion, and measurable accountability pressure across affected systems.
description_long: The Guardian reported that U.S. and Israeli forces intensified attacks on Iran on March 3, 2026, targeting command facilities, government sites and missile-launch locations. Donald Trump said on Truth Social that Iran wanted to talk and that he had rejected the approach as too late. Iran’s ambassador to the United Nations in Geneva denied that Tehran had sought negotiations, leaving the claimed overture disputed. Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned that the “hardest hits are yet to come,” while Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth raised the possibility of U.S. troops on the ground. Iran launched missile and drone attacks across the Gulf, including against U.S. bases, embassies and civilian infrastructure. The Guardian reported the Red Crescent’s figure of 787 deaths in Iran and described damage to energy and transport sites and rising energy prices. U.S. officials gave differing accounts of the war’s aims, including preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and changing its leadership. The report records escalation and competing public accounts; it does not show that formal negotiations had begun.

title: Trump administration warns tariff refund process ‘will take time’
description_short: Trump administration warns tariff refund process ‘will take time’
description_medium: Trump administration warns tariff refund process ‘will take time’. DoJ says it will not ask US supreme court to rehear tariffs case despite president’s complaint on Truth Social This entry is cataloged as a standalone event because it captures a concrete action, public statement, or policy consequence linked directly to Trump. The downstream effects include elevated institutional stress, public-trust erosion, and measurable accountability pressure across affected systems.
description_long: The Guardian reported that the Justice Department told a court the tariff-refund process would take time after the Supreme Court invalidated most of the administration’s country-specific tariffs imposed under the 1977 emergency-powers law. FedEx and hundreds of other importers had sought repayment, including companies that filed claims before the ruling. The Court held that the emergency-powers statute did not authorize most of the tariffs at issue. DOJ did not ask the justices to rehear the case, even after Trump publicly complained about the ruling and suggested a rehearing. The administration argued that refunds would create an undeserved windfall for companies and foreign countries, while officials considered other legal authorities for replacement tariffs. The report describes the government’s response to the Court’s decision and an unresolved claims process. It does not establish a final refund schedule, the amount each importer would receive or the total ultimately paid. The announcement that repayment would take time is therefore not evidence that refunds were denied or that every claimant was eligible.

title: Trump: Maine university pulls support from conference on Palestine, citing Trump sanctions
description_short: Trump: Maine university pulls support from conference on Palestine, citing Trump sanctions
description_medium: Maine university pulls support from conference on Palestine, citing Trump sanctions. Organizers scramble for new venue after University of Southern Maine cites sanctions over Francesca Albanese’s virtual talk This entry is cataloged as a standalone event because it captures a concrete action, public statement, or policy consequence linked directly to Trump. The downstream effects include elevated institutional stress, public-trust erosion, and measurable accountability pressure across affected systems.
description_long: The Guardian reported that the University of Southern Maine withdrew access to an on-campus venue days before the “Consequences of Palestine” conference, citing the planned remote participation of Francesca Albanese, the U.N. special rapporteur for the occupied Palestinian territories. The Trump administration had sanctioned Albanese the previous July. More than 300 people had registered, and organizers searched for another venue after the university ended its support. A university system official argued that hosting an event featuring a sanctioned speaker could violate federal law. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control had issued guidance in December stating that remote participation by Albanese, without payment or other prohibited services, did not require prior authorization. Organizers offered to remove her from the program, but the university said there was insufficient time to assess the event’s risk. A professor involved in the conference said administrators had raised concerns about possible federal funding cuts; the university denied acting in response to political pressure and said it had ended its contract before receiving a letter from Republican lawmakers. The report documents a local venue decision and differing legal explanations, but not a direction from Trump or the conference’s eventual outcome.

title: Trump: Half of Americans back abolishing ICE amid Trump crackdown, poll finds
description_short: Trump: Half of Americans back abolishing ICE amid Trump crackdown, poll finds
description_medium: Half of Americans back abolishing ICE amid Trump crackdown, poll finds. YouGov poll shows 50% support as Kristi Noem defends ‘terrorist’ claim and shutdown drags on This entry is cataloged as a standalone event because it captures a concrete action, public statement, or policy consequence linked directly to Trump. The downstream effects include elevated institutional stress, public-trust erosion, and measurable accountability pressure across affected systems.
description_long: The Economist/YouGov poll, conducted from February 27 through March 2, 2026, found that half of respondents somewhat or strongly supported abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement, while 39% opposed it. Support reached 77% among Democrats and 52% among independents; 68% of Republicans opposed abolition. The survey also asked about specific practices: 75% favored requiring ICE officers to wear identifying uniforms, 59% opposed allowing agents to hide their faces with masks, 58% said the agency used excessive force, and 44% said they had no confidence in ICE. The Guardian placed those views amid Trump administration enforcement operations and a partial Department of Homeland Security shutdown, including scrutiny of Secretary Kristi Noem after the Minneapolis deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti. The results show public opinion at a particular point during the dispute over immigration enforcement. The available poll page does not provide the sample size or full questionnaire and methodology, so the precise wording and survey design cannot be assessed from the supplied information.

title: Most Americans Said Trump's Iran War Wasn't Going Well
description_short: Most Americans Said Trump's Iran War Wasn't Going Well
description_medium: A CBS poll found most Americans thought the Iran war was not going well, even as many Republicans and especially MAGA voters kept expressing confidence in Trump himself. That split matters because it shows how personal loyalty keeps overpowering plain evidence. The war can look bad, feel bad, and still remain protected inside the cult.
description_long: CBS News and YouGov surveyed 3,335 U.S. adults from March 17 through 20, 2026, with a reported margin of error of 2.1 percentage points. Most respondents said the Iran conflict was not going well and characterized it as a war of choice rather than a necessity. Many said the administration had not clearly explained its goals, wanted the fighting to end quickly, and connected the conflict with higher gasoline prices and concern about the economy. Most did not expect the war to improve the U.S. economy, and a little over one-third thought it would make the country safer over the long term. Views differed by party: Republicans, particularly MAGA voters, expressed more support for Trump and the military action, while disapproval was more common among Democrats and independents. The poll records opinion during the conflict, not battlefield outcomes or a future policy decision. The poll provides a dated snapshot of public attitudes during the conflict; it does not measure battlefield outcomes or determine what policy the administration would pursue next.

title: Trump's Deportation Machine Was So Warehousing-Obsessed DHS Had to Pause New Immigrant Holding Deals
description_short: Trump's Deportation Machine Was So Warehousing-Obsessed DHS Had to Pause New Immigrant Holding Deals
description_medium: PBS reported that DHS paused the purchase of new warehouses meant to hold immigrants while it reviewed contracts signed during the department's most scandal-soaked stretch. The pause does not redeem the policy. It reveals the scale and crudity of what Trump built: an industrial detention pipeline where migrants become inventory, storage space becomes strategy, and administrative excess is just another word for planned cruelty.
description_long: PBS NewsHour, carrying an Associated Press report, said on April 1, 2026, that the Department of Homeland Security had paused purchases of additional warehouses intended for immigrant detention while it reviewed contracts signed under former secretary Kristi Noem. The review also covered completed purchases: DHS had spent a combined $1.074 billion on 11 warehouses in eight states. The department had inherited a separate $38.3 billion plan to expand detention capacity to 92,000 beds through large detention centers and regional processing sites. The warehouse purchases faced local opposition over the facilities and potential demands on water and sewer systems; lawsuits were pending in three states, and some proposed sales fell through when owners declined to sell. The pause followed Markwayne Mullin’s arrival as DHS secretary. It applied to new acquisitions and contract review. It did not show that existing warehouses would close or that the administration had abandoned its broader detention-expansion plan. The report describes a contract review and detention-expansion plan, not DHS’s motive for purchasing the warehouses.

title: Trump Claimed Iranians Welcomed US Infrastructure Strikes Without Proof
description_short: Trump Claimed Iranians Welcomed US Infrastructure Strikes Without Proof
description_medium: At a White House press conference on April 6, 2026, Donald Trump said intercepted communications showed Iranians near bombing sites urging U.S. forces to continue striking. The Guardian report provided no evidence for the alleged intercepts. Trump argued that civilians would accept losing power and other services to escape Iran’s government, while threatening attacks on energy facilities and bridges if the Strait of Hormuz stayed closed.
description_long: The Guardian reported that Donald Trump claimed on April 6, 2026, that Iranian civilians welcomed U.S. strikes on infrastructure. At a White House press conference, he said intercepted communications showed people near active bombing sites urging U.S. forces to continue, but the report supplied no evidence for the alleged intercepts. Trump argued that civilians would accept losing electricity and other services to escape Iran’s government, invoking the 2022 “Woman, Life, Freedom” protests. He dismissed concerns that strikes on infrastructure would punish civilians and threatened attacks on energy facilities and bridges if Iran did not reopen the Strait of Hormuz by an 8 p.m. Tuesday deadline. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the day’s attacks would be the largest volume since the operation began. Democratic lawmakers and Iran’s U.N. mission warned that attacks on civilian infrastructure could violate the laws of war; those were objections to threatened targets, not a court finding about a completed strike. The report documents Trump’s assertion and threat, not proof that Iranians welcomed the attacks or that the threatened strikes occurred.
